docs.title: libc
docs.text:
libc is a binding layer that exposes the C standard library, POSIX and Linux system calls to Mojo through external_call.

Every header gets its own sub-package, so you import only what you need:

libc.math      libc.string     libc.stdio      libc.stdlib
libc.unistd    libc.dirent     libc.time       libc.signal
libc.pthread   libc.network    libc.sys.*      ...

docs.title: Status
docs.text: The package is developed against Mojo 1.1.0 and is published to the mojo-force channel on prefix.dev. It is exercised on Linux (x86-64) and macOS (Apple silicon).

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from libc.math import sqrt
from libc.string import strlen
from libc.utils import string_to_char_ptr


def main() raises:
    print(sqrt(2.0))

    var ptr = string_to_char_ptr("hello")
    print(strlen(ptr))
    ptr.unsafe_free()

Memory and environment come from libc.stdlib:

from libc.stdlib import atoi, free, malloc
from libc.utils import string_to_char_ptr


def main():
    var block = malloc(8)
    block.unsafe_store(0, 65)
    _ = free(block)

    var digits = string_to_char_ptr("512")
    print(atoi(digits))
    digits.unsafe_free()

See Install and Usage for the details.

docs.title: What is here that C does not have
docs.text:
This is a binding, so what it can call is a subset of what C can call and will stay that way. The count says how much of a subset: libc, libm, libdl and librt publish 2778 functions between them, and this binds 567 C symbols, 562 of which are among those — 20.2%. C offers more, and calling more of it is not what this is for.

(567 took correcting. An earlier count here said 470, because the symbol was read off the same line as external_call[ and a fifth of the calls in this package put the name on the next line instead. The honest number was higher, and nobody benefited from the lower one.)

The rest of this page is about the other question, which is not "how much" but "how". There are things C cannot do for the caller, or does by convention and hope, and a binding can do them properly because it gets to choose what the call looks like on this side.

docs.title: Asking what a number means
docs.text:
errno is a number at run time and a macro at compile time, and nothing in C joins the two. A program prints 2 and whoever reads it looks ENOENT up in a table, because there is no errno_name in libc to ask.

There is one here:

from libc.errno import check, errno_message, errno_name

print(errno_name(2))            # ENOENT
print(errno_message(2))         # ENOENT: No such file or directory

var fd = check(open(path, O_RDONLY))          # raises instead of answering -1
var stream = check_ptr(fopen(path, mode))     # and for the calls that answer NULL

check covers the half of libc that says -1; check_ptr covers the other half, the one that says NULL — fopen, malloc, getcwd — for which a test against a negative number says nothing. C has no answer to either, having no exceptions to raise: the nearest it comes is a macro of one's own that calls perror and then exit, which is not the same as being able to catch it.

errno_name answers for the platform it was built for. EAGAIN is 11 here and 35 on Darwin, and it says EAGAIN either way.

docs.title: Macros that are functions
docs.text: WIFEXITED, WEXITSTATUS, WIFSIGNALED, WTERMSIG, WIFSTOPPED, WSTOPSIG and WCOREDUMP are macros in C, which is to say they are text substitution: no types, no way to name one or pass it along, nothing for a debugger to step into. Here they are functions, and they were checked the only way worth checking — against glibc's macros, for all 65536 possible statuses, and they agree on every one.

docs.title: Differences that are visible instead of hidden
docs.text:
C handles a difference between platforms with #ifdef, and the reader of the header sees one of the two answers and not the fact that there was a choice. This writes the choice out:

comptime EAGAIN = 35 if CompilationTarget.is_macos() else 11

and then proves it on both, because CI runs on both. EAGAIN is the one worth watching: a value that is not the platform's own fails a test here rather than in somebody's error handling.

docs.title: A check that runs against C itself
docs.text:
This is the one with no counterpart. scripts/check-prototypes.py compares the binding against C on this machine: every call is compared against the C prototype — 601 of them now, each compiled from the header on this machine — and a mismatch is reported rather than found later.

And now scripts/check-constants.py does the same for the numbers. It includes every header either script knows, asks C to print each constant, and compares: 553 of them at this writing, of which 52 are written as expressions (S_IRUSR | S_IWUSR) rather than as numbers, so those are handed to C whole and a misspelled name inside one fails to compile. It runs on both platforms in CI, which is the point of it — the platform decides which side of an if is_macos() is under trial, and neither job can check the branch it is not standing on.

It earned its place on the first run. Fifty-five constants were Darwin's values with no platform branch at all: O_APPEND was 8, which is what Darwin says and not what Linux says, Linux saying 1024, and the same for O_CREAT, O_TRUNC, every LOG_* and most of F_*. None of it failed a test, because nothing here asserted what the number meant — open received 512 where 64 was intended and created something other than was asked for, quietly, in the way these things do. A number read off gcc -dM by eye is right exactly once, and that was a long time ago.

And scripts/check-layouts.py asks C how big each struct is and where it has to start, which tests/test_layout.mojo had been doing for thirty-two things about eight structs and nothing for the rest. Its first run found six wrong. Five were opaque blocks held as Array[UInt8, N] — fenv_t, fexcept_t, pthread_attr_t, pthread_condattr_t, mbstate_t — and a row of single bytes asks to be aligned on no boundary at all, so every call taking one was handed a pointer C asks for four or eight and never agreed to be given one byte off. Those now sit in words.

The sixth was qelem, which is not opaque: it names the two links and nothing else, which made it sixteen bytes to C's twenty-four, because C's declares a third member, char q_data[1], trailing after them. Nothing here ever looked at those eight bytes, so insque and remque work either way — until you put one next to anything else and it writes into the gap. A struct used for its size and never read has to be the right size for the reason that it is used for its size.

Being larger than C needs is not a mistake and half of them are: an opaque block sized for whichever of the two platforms wanted most costs bytes and breaks nothing, since every call takes it by pointer and libc writes less than it was given. The script says which is which rather than treating any difference as failure.

Field offsets are still on trust. size_of and align_of reach Mojo without constructing anything; the offset of a member does not, because asking a pointer where a member lives asks for a member pointer, and Mojo has none. That leaves 116 fields whose positions are whatever they were written down as.

glibc, for its part, does not come with anything that checks glibc.

docs.title: Next to Rust's libc
docs.text:
The nearest thing to this that is not this: rust-lang/libc. It binds the same C and implements none of it, which is what this does too. Four of its Linux files declare 681 C functions; this binds 567; 293 are in both.

The difference is not the count. Rust answers "what is EAGAIN" with a file per platform and a cfg that picks one, so the answer for the platform you are not on is somewhere else in the tree. This writes both numbers on one line and runs CI on both. Rust supports more platforms than two, and this supports two and proves both — which is the trade, stated as the trade rather than as a win.

docs.title: One thing that is awkward, and said out loud
docs.text: Mojo's pointers are non-null by design: Bool(ptr) is refused, and the type says a pointer always points at something. C's half of the binding does not share that opinion, and a call that fails answers with NULL whatever the type says, so NULL is what arrives — a pointer whose address is 0. check_ptr turns it into an exception, and Int is how it sees it, being the one way left to ask.

docs.title: What C does and this does not
docs.text:
Being fair about the other direction:

  • Variadic functions. printf, scanf, fcntl, ioctl. An external call has to name every type it passes, and C's own variadic convention on arm64 Darwin passes on the stack, where the call cannot reach.
  • Callbacks. Nothing here can hand C a function pointer, so qsort, bsearch and signal handlers are out.
  • Coverage. 16.7%, as above. open here is bound as openat with AT_FDCWD filled in, which is what POSIX says the two amount to, and is the sort of thing that happens when the real name cannot be called.
  • Variadic arguments, and the argument after them. openat is variadic too, so the mode is not a named argument on macOS either and does not arrive: a file asked for with 0o644 came out as 0o150, which is no umask of 0o644 but whatever was on the stack. fchmod afterwards is the way to be sure, and both docstrings say so.
  • Speed. Measured, and there is nothing here to be modest about: 1.6 ns per call through the binding against 2.2 ns for the same call from C — strlen, 20 million times, run twice. The gap favours neither in any way that means anything: the C side pays for a jump through the procedure linkage table that an external call does not, and the spread between two runs of the same binary is wider than the distance between the two numbers. scripts/bench-call.sh prints both.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: libc is distributed as a conda package that installs a precompiled Mojo package (libc.mojoc) into your environment's lib/mojo directory, so import libc resolves without extra flags.

docs.title: pixi
docs.text:
pixi add --from https://conda.modular.com/max --channel mojo-force libc

or, in pixi.toml:

[workspace]
channels = ["https://conda.modular.com/max", "conda-forge", "mojo-force"]

[dependencies]
libc = ">=0.12.0,<0.13"
mojo = ">=1.1.0,<2"

docs.title: conda / mamba
docs.text: conda install -c https://conda.modular.com/max -c mojo-force libc

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/mojothon/libc.git
cd libc
pixi run test            # run the test suite
pixi run package         # build dist/libc.mojoc

To consume a source checkout directly, point the compiler at src:

mojo run -I src your_program.mojo

Note

A precompiled .mojoc package is tied to the compiler version that produced it. Rebuild the package (or use the source checkout) after upgrading Mojo.

docs.text:

docs.title: Not started yet
docs.text:
libc.threads (<threads.h>) exports nothing: Apple never shipped C11 threads, so a binding would only ever work on Linux.

libc.math has no long double variants — no fabsl, no nexttoward — because Mojo has no type to pass: on x86-64 the C type is the 80-bit x87 format. libc.locale has no FE_DFL_ENV, see fenv_t.

libc.sys.epoll, libc.sys.prctl, libc.sys.sendfile, libc.sys.auxv and libc.sys.random wrap Linux-only calls; importing them on Darwin will not link.

libc.stdio covers the <stdio.h> entry points that libc.file does not already own; see the note at the top of src/libc/stdio/syscalls.mojo. libc.complex models double complex and float complex as the two-field structs the ABI actually passes; long double complex is left out because Mojo has no 80-bit type.

docs.title: The six no test asks for
docs.text:
Six of the bindings are never called by a test, and cannot be:

Call Why not libc.file.ioctl Variadic: which device it is and what it is asked to do both come after the arguments that can be given. libc.file.scanf Reads from standard input, which a test cannot promise will ever come to an end. libc.signal.sigsuspend Waits for a signal to arrive. A test that waits is a test that stops. libc.signal.sigwait The same. Given a set with nothing in it, glibc waits rather than refusing. libc.stdio.getchar Reads from standard input, as scanf does. libc.unistd.pause Waits for a signal.

None of them is known to be broken; they are simply not asked. A test that hung, or that ended the process running it, would be worse than no test at all.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
Generate the docstring reference for any module with the Mojo toolchain:

mojo doc src/libc/unistd/syscalls.mojo

docs.title: Calling a C function
docs.text:
Each module mirrors one C header. Functions keep their C names and are thin external_call wrappers, so the arguments and return values match the C prototype:

from libc.unistd import getpid, getuid


def main():
    print(getpid(), getuid())

docs.title: Strings
docs.text:
C APIs take char *. libc.utils converts between Mojo String and a NUL terminated buffer:

from libc.utils import CString, char_ptr_to_string, string_to_char_ptr, strlen


def main() raises:
    var ptr = string_to_char_ptr("hello, libc")
    print(strlen(ptr))              # 11
    print(char_ptr_to_string(ptr))  # hello, libc

    var view = CString(ptr)         # borrowed view, printable
    print(view)

    ptr.unsafe_free()               # you own the buffer

string_to_char_ptr() allocates; release the result with unsafe_free(). Pointers returned by C (for example opendir()) must be released with the matching C function instead.

docs.title: Pointers
docs.text:
Raw pointers are spelled c_ptr[T], an alias for Pointer[T, MutUntrackedOrigin]:

from libc.constant import c_ptr


def read_first(p: c_ptr[UInt8]) -> UInt8:
    return p.unsafe_load(0)

Point at a Mojo value with Pointer(to=value) when a C API needs an out parameter.

docs.title: NULL
docs.text:
Mojo pointers are not nullable, so there is no spelling of NULL and nothing to compare one against. libc.utils covers both directions:

  • null_ptr[T]() builds one to hand in, where C says a null pointer will do — strtok carrying on from where it was, time when only its answer is wanted, nanosleep when the remainder does not matter.
  • is_null() asks whether one that came back is NULL, which is how fopen, opendir, dlopen and most of the rest say they failed.
from libc.dirent import closedir, opendir
from libc.utils import is_null, null_ptr, string_to_char_ptr


def main() raises:
    var path = string_to_char_ptr("/does/not/exist")
    var dirp = opendir(path)
    if is_null(dirp):
        print("no such directory")
    else:
        _ = closedir(dirp)
    path.unsafe_free()

Never read through a null pointer. Handing one in is only ever for C to notice and take the other branch.

docs.title: Structs
docs.text:
Structures are declared with the field layout of the corresponding C struct. Trivial ones conform to TrivialRegisterPassable, so they can be passed and returned by value:

from libc.dirent import closedir, opendir, readdir
from libc.utils import string_to_char_ptr


def main() raises:
    var path = string_to_char_ptr("/tmp")
    var dirp = opendir(path)
    var entry = readdir(dirp)
    print(entry[].name())
    _ = closedir(dirp)
    path.unsafe_free()

Warning

struct dirent is held as raw bytes and read through ino(), reclen(), type() and name(). Its d_name is an inline character array, not a pointer, and the two platforms do not put it in the same place: it sits at offset 19 on glibc and 12 on Darwin, with d_type at 18 and 10. Reading it as a pointer, or guessing one offset for both, yields a garbage address or a name taken from the wrong bytes.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text:
libc.constant carries the C type aliases (c_int, c_size_t, ...) plus the O_*, SEEK_*, AT_* and errno values:

from libc.constant import O_CREAT, O_RDWR, SEEK_END

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Most wrappers return the raw C value: -1 (or NULL) on failure with errno set. Read it with libc.errno.get_errno().

docs.title: Version
docs.text:
libc.__version__ 0.12.0 Mojo >=1.1.0,<2 Platforms linux-64, osx-arm64 
from libc import __version__


def main():
    print(__version__)

The version lives in src/libc/version.mojo and is mirrored in pixi.toml and recipe/recipe.yaml. Bump all three together.

See CHANGELOG for the release history.
